name: Two pointers
blurb: On a sorted row, put one finger at each end. If the pair adds up to too little, move the left finger right. Too much, move the right finger left. You never check every pair.
code: left ← first; right ← last
while left < right
sum ← a[left] + a[right]
if sum = target: found
if sum is too small: left → right
else: right → left
no pair adds up

offline.title: Pair up
offline.need: Number cards in order, and a target number
steps: Lay 8 number cards face up in order, smallest on the left.
Pick a target. Put one finger on the first card and one on the last.
Add the two cards. Too small? Move the left finger right. Too big? Move the right finger left.
Stop when they add to the target, or when your fingers meet.
offline.think: Why can you safely ignore a card once its finger has moved past it?

name: Sliding window
blurb: To find the best run of 3 in a row, do not re-add every run. Slide the window one step: add the number that comes in, take away the one that leaves.
code: sum ← first k numbers; best ← sum
for each next number
sum ← sum + new − the one leaving
best ← the larger of best and sum
answer is best

offline.title: Slide the frame
offline.need: A strip of squared paper with numbers, and a card with a 3-square window cut out
steps: Write 9 numbers in a row on the strip.
Put the window over the first 3 and add them.
Slide the window one place. Do not add again: add the new number, take away the one that left.
Keep the best total. Slide to the end.
offline.think: How many additions does each slide need, compared with adding all 3 from scratch? What if the window were 100 wide?

name: Prefix sums
blurb: Add up the row once, keeping a running total. After that, the sum of any stretch is just one subtraction: the total at the end minus the total just before the start.
code: for each i: P[i+1] ← P[i] + a[i]
sum of a[l..r] ← P[r+1] − P[l]

offline.title: Running total
offline.need: Paper and a pencil
steps: Write 8 numbers in a row. Under them, write a running total: each box is the box before plus the number above.
Pick two positions. The sum between them is the running total at the end minus the running total just before the start.
Check by adding the numbers one by one. They agree.
offline.think: If you had to answer 1000 questions about the same row, why is the running total worth building first?

name: Binary search on the answer
blurb: You can binary-search more than a sorted list. If you can test a guess (is this speed fast enough?) and bigger guesses never do worse, halve the range of possible answers.
code: low ← 1; high ← biggest possible
while low < high
mid ← the middle guess
if mid works: high ← mid
else: low ← mid + 1
answer is low

offline.title: Slowest speed that works
offline.need: Paper, a pencil and 4 piles of coins
steps: Make 4 piles of coins. You may eat from one pile per hour, up to your speed. You have H hours.
Guess a speed in the middle. Work out how many hours it takes (each pile needs its size divided by speed, rounded up).
Fast enough? Try a slower speed. Too slow? Try faster. Always guess the middle of what is left.
Stop when only one speed is left.
offline.think: Why can you throw away half the speeds after each test?

name: Counting sort
blurb: When the numbers are small, you do not need to compare at all. Count how many times each number appears, then write each number out as many times as you counted.
code: counts ← zeros for 0 … max
for each number: counts[number] += 1
for each value 0 … max
write it counts[value] times

offline.title: Sort by counting
offline.need: 20 playing cards, or numbers 0 to 5 on paper slips
steps: Draw 6 boxes labelled 0 to 5.
Take each number in turn and put a tally mark in its box.
Read the boxes from 0 to 5. Write each number as many times as it has tally marks.
The list is sorted, and you never compared two numbers.
offline.think: Why would this stop working for numbers up to a billion?

name: Radix sort
blurb: Sort by the last digit first, using ten buckets and keeping the order. Then sort by the tens digit the same way. After the last digit, the whole row is sorted.
code: for each digit place, last digit first:
put each number in the bucket for its digit
collect the buckets in order, 0 to 9
sorted after the last place

offline.title: Bucket shuffle
offline.need: Ten cups labelled 0 to 9 and 8 two-digit number cards
steps: Put each card in the cup that matches its last digit. Add cards on top, so the order inside a cup is kept.
Collect the cards cup by cup, from 0 to 9, keeping each cup in order.
Now put each card in the cup for its first digit, and collect again.
The cards are in order.
offline.think: Why must the second round keep the order from the first round inside each cup?

name: Monotonic stacks
blurb: For each number, find the next bigger number to its right. Keep a stack of numbers still waiting. A new number that is bigger than the top answers it, and lets it leave.
code: stack ← empty
for each number n, left to right
while the top is smaller than n:
answer for the top ← n; pop it
push n
whatever is left has no bigger number

offline.title: Waiting in line
offline.need: A row of 7 number cards and a small pile area
steps: Turn over the cards one at a time from the left. Keep a pile of cards still waiting for something bigger.
When the new card is bigger than the top of the pile, the top has found its answer. Take it off, write the new card next to it.
Keep taking cards off while the new card is bigger. Then put the new card on the pile.
Cards left on the pile never found a bigger one.
offline.think: Each card goes on the pile once and off once. What does that tell you about how much work it is?

name: Deques
blurb: A deque is a line you can add to or remove from at both ends. To find the biggest number in every window, keep only the numbers that might still win and drop the smaller ones behind a bigger newcomer.
code: deque ← empty (holds positions)
for each number n
drop from the BACK while the back is ≤ n
add n at the back
drop from the FRONT if it left the window
the front is the window maximum

offline.title: Candidates in a queue
offline.need: 9 number cards and a strip of paper
steps: Lay 9 cards in a row. We want the biggest in every 3 in a row.
Keep a short queue of candidates. A new card removes any smaller cards from the back, then joins the back.
If the front card has slid out of the window, remove it.
The front card is the biggest in the window. Write it down.
offline.think: Why can a smaller card behind a bigger one never be the biggest again?

name: Strings: palindromes
blurb: A palindrome reads the same backwards. Check it with two pointers: compare the first and last letters, then move inward. One mismatch ends it.
code: left ← first; right ← last
while left < right
if letters differ: not a palindrome
left ← left + 1; right ← right − 1
every pair matched: palindrome

offline.title: Mirror words
offline.need: Letter tiles or paper slips
steps: Spell RACECAR with tiles in a row.
Point at the first and last tile. Do they match? Move both fingers inward.
Try PENCIL and LEVEL. Stop at the first mismatch.
offline.think: How many comparisons does a word of 100 letters need at most?

name: Cycle detection
blurb: Is a chain of links a loop? Send a slow walker (1 step) and a fast walker (2 steps). On a loop the fast one catches the slow one. On a straight chain the fast one runs off the end.
code: slow ← head; fast ← head
while fast and fast.next exist
slow ← slow.next
fast ← fast.next.next
if slow = fast: a cycle!
fast ran off the end: no cycle

offline.title: Tortoise and hare
offline.need: A drawing of 7 dots joined by arrows, and two coins
steps: Draw 7 dots with arrows between them. Make the last arrow go back to an earlier dot, or leave it out.
Put two coins on the first dot. Each turn, move one coin one arrow and the other coin two arrows.
If the coins meet, there is a loop. If one coin runs off the end, there is not.
offline.think: Why must the fast coin catch the slow one if there is a loop?

name: Linked lists: reverse
blurb: A linked list is a chain of boxes, each knowing only the next one. To reverse it, walk along and turn each arrow around to point at the box behind it.
code: previous ← nothing; current ← head
while current exists
next ← current.next (remember it!)
current.next ← previous
previous ← current; current ← next
previous is the new head

offline.title: Turn the arrows
offline.need: 5 cards in a row and string or pencil arrows
steps: Lay 5 cards in a row with an arrow from each card to the next.
Start at the first card. Remember where its arrow pointed, then turn its arrow to point backward.
Move to the card you remembered and repeat.
When you finish, the chain runs the other way.
offline.think: What goes wrong if you turn an arrow before remembering where it pointed?

name: Matrices and grids
blurb: A grid is a list of rows. To visit it in a spiral, go right until the edge, then down, left and up. Turn whenever the next square is off the grid or already visited.
code: direction ← right
repeat rows × columns times
visit this square
if the next square is off the grid or visited: turn clockwise
step forward

offline.title: Spiral walk
offline.need: Squared paper (3 rows by 4 columns) and a pencil
steps: Draw a grid 4 across and 3 down and write 1 to 12 in order.
Start in the top-left. Go right until you cannot, then down, then left, then up.
Cross out squares as you visit them. Turn whenever the next square is crossed out or is off the grid.
Write the numbers in the order you visited them.
offline.think: How does the spiral know when it has finished?

name: Amortised cost
blurb: A growing list lives in a box with spare room. Adding is cheap until the box is full. Then everything is copied into a box twice as big. That copy is rare, so adding stays cheap on average.
code: if the box is full:
make a box twice as big
copy everything across
put the new item in
average cost = total work ÷ adds

offline.title: The doubling shelf
offline.need: Paper cups and small objects
steps: Start with a row of 1 cup. Put an object in.
When the row is full and you want to add another, lay out a row twice as long and carry every object across. Count each carry.
Add 9 objects in all. Count every placement and every carry.
Divide the total by 9.
offline.think: Why is it better to double the space than to add just one more cup each time?

name: Invariants
blurb: An invariant is a promise that stays true every time round a loop. In insertion sort the promise is that everything left of the arrow is in order. If every step keeps the promise, the end is sorted.
code: invariant: a[0 … i−1] is sorted
for i = 1 … n−1
take a[i] out
slide bigger numbers right
drop it in the gap
(invariant: a[0 … i] is sorted)

offline.title: Keep the promise
offline.need: A hand of 6 playing cards
steps: Hold the cards in a row. The first card on its own is already "sorted".
Take the next card and slide it left into place among the cards already sorted.
After each card, check: is everything to the left of my finger in order?
When your finger reaches the end, all cards are in order.
offline.think: What would break if you inserted a card into the wrong place once?

name: Steps and loops
blurb: A computer does one small step at a time. A loop repeats the same steps. Adding 1 to 6 is a loop: take the next number, add it to a running total, repeat.
code: total ← 0
for each number from 1 to n
total ← total + number
the answer is total

offline.title: Be the loop
offline.need: Paper and a pencil
steps: Write total = 0 on paper.
Add 1, cross out the old total, write the new one. Then add 2, then 3, up to 6.
You are the loop: same step, repeated, with a memory.
offline.think: How many steps would adding 1 to 1,000 take?

name: Best, worst and average case
blurb: The same method can be lucky or unlucky. Opening boxes one by one is fastest when the target is in the first box. It is slowest when the target is last or missing. On average it takes about half the boxes.
code: for each box from the left
open it
if it holds the target: stop
not found: every box was opened

offline.title: Luck of the draw
offline.need: 8 cards face down in a row, and a friend
steps: Lay 8 cards in a row, face down. Pick a target card.
Open from the left until you find it. Count the cards opened.
Repeat 8 times with the target in a different place each time (first, second, … last).
Add up the counts and divide by 8. That is the average case.
offline.think: Why do we usually plan for the worst case, even though it is the least likely?

name: Space and time
blurb: You can often swap memory for speed. Checking if a number is prime by dividing takes many steps each time. Write all the answers in a table once, and every question after that takes one look.
code: slow way: test by dividing, every question
fast way: build a table of answers first
each question: look it up in the table
more memory, less time

offline.title: The answer sheet
offline.need: Paper and a pencil
steps: Pick 5 numbers up to 30. For each, test whether it is prime by dividing by 2, 3, 4, 5 and counting your divisions.
Now write a list of all the primes up to 30 once (your table).
Check the same 5 numbers by looking in the table. Count your looks.
Which was faster for 5 questions? For 5,000?
offline.think: When is it not worth building the table?

name: Sqrt decomposition
blurb: Cut a long row into blocks and write down each block's total. To add up a stretch, use the written totals for whole blocks and add the few loose numbers at the ends.
code: split the row into blocks of 3; write each block's total
query(l, r):
add single numbers until the start of a block
add whole block totals while a block fits
add single numbers for the ragged end

offline.title: Chunked sums
offline.need: Paper with 9 numbers in three boxes of three
steps: Write 9 numbers. Draw a box round each group of 3 and write the group total beneath it.
Pick a stretch such as the 2nd to the 8th number.
Add the loose numbers at each end one by one, and use the written total for any full box in between.
Check with a slow sum.
offline.think: How many additions does this use compared with adding the whole stretch?

name: Mo's algorithm
blurb: You have lots of questions about stretches of a row. Keep one window and slide its ends instead of starting over each time. Answer the questions in a smart order so the window barely moves.
code: sort the questions by (block of the left end, right end)
for each question in that order
move the left end to the question's left, adding or removing one number at a time
move the right end the same way
the window now holds exactly the question's stretch: read the answer

offline.title: Sliding frame
offline.need: A strip of 9 numbers from 1 to 4, and a card with a window
steps: Write 9 numbers from 1 to 4. Make a tally of which numbers are in the window.
Take 4 questions of the form "how many different numbers are between place l and place r?".
Instead of re-counting each from scratch, slide the window ends from the last question to the next, adding or removing one number each step and updating the tally.
Count your steps and compare with counting every stretch from scratch.
offline.think: Why does sorting the questions make the window move less overall?

name: Recursion
blurb: A function can solve a problem by calling itself on a smaller version. 5! is 5 times 4!, and so on down to 1!, which is just 1. That smallest case is the base case. Then each waiting call finishes on the way back up.
code: factorial(n):
if n is 1: answer 1 (the base case)
otherwise: ask factorial(n − 1)
when it answers: multiply by n
give that answer back

offline.title: Russian dolls
offline.need: A set of nesting dolls (or 5 cups that stack), paper and a pencil
steps: Open the biggest doll. Inside is a smaller one: open that. Keep going until the smallest, which holds nothing. That is the base case.
Now close them back up from the smallest. Each time, you finish the job for that doll.
Write 5! as 5 × 4!, 4! as 4 × 3!, and so on down to 1. Then work back up multiplying.
Notice you needed to remember every unfinished doll on the way down.
offline.think: What would happen if the dolls never ended, with no smallest one?

name: Recursion: the call tree
blurb: Each Fibonacci number is the two before it added together. Written as recursion, every call makes two more calls, and the same small questions get asked again and again. The tree of calls shows the waste.
facts: The same fib asked many times
code: fib(n):
if n is 0 or 1: answer n (the base case)
otherwise: ask fib(n − 1) and fib(n − 2)
add the two answers
give the sum back

offline.title: Draw the calls
offline.need: Paper and a pencil
steps: Draw fib(5) at the top. Under it draw its two calls, fib(4) and fib(3). Keep drawing each call's two calls until you reach fib(1) or fib(0).
Count the circles. How many say fib(2)? How many say fib(3)?
Write the answer in each circle from the bottom up.
Now think: how could you avoid answering fib(2) more than once?
offline.think: If fib(5) needs 15 calls, roughly how many would fib(10) need? What would writing answers down save?

name: Preorder traversal
blurb: Visit a node first, then everything on its left, then everything on its right. Good for copying a tree.
code: visit the node
preorder(left)
preorder(right)

offline.title: Walk the tree
offline.need: A tree drawn on paper with 7 numbers, and a finger
steps: Draw a tree with 7 numbers: one at the top, and up to two below each.
Follow the rule: node, left, right. Say each number out loud as you "visit" it.
Write the numbers in the order you said them.
Try the other three orders on the same tree. Are the lists the same?
offline.think: Which order gives a sorted list on a search tree?

name: Inorder traversal
blurb: Everything on the left, then the node, then everything on the right. On a search tree this reads the numbers from smallest to biggest.
code: inorder(left)
visit the node
inorder(right)

offline.title: Walk the tree
offline.need: A tree drawn on paper with 7 numbers, and a finger
steps: Draw a tree with 7 numbers: one at the top, and up to two below each.
Follow the rule: left, node, right. Say each number out loud as you "visit" it.
Write the numbers in the order you said them.
Try the other three orders on the same tree. Are the lists the same?
offline.think: Which order gives a sorted list on a search tree?

name: Postorder traversal
blurb: Left, then right, then the node last. A node is visited only after all of its children. Good for deleting a tree.
code: postorder(left)
postorder(right)
visit the node

offline.title: Walk the tree
offline.need: A tree drawn on paper with 7 numbers, and a finger
steps: Draw a tree with 7 numbers: one at the top, and up to two below each.
Follow the rule: left, right, node. Say each number out loud as you "visit" it.
Write the numbers in the order you said them.
Try the other three orders on the same tree. Are the lists the same?
offline.think: Which order gives a sorted list on a search tree?

name: Level order traversal
blurb: Visit the tree row by row, top to bottom, left to right, using a queue. Good for finding the nearest node.
code: queue ← [root]
take the front node and visit it
add its children at the back

offline.title: Walk the tree
offline.need: A tree drawn on paper with 7 numbers, and a finger
steps: Draw a tree with 7 numbers: one at the top, and up to two below each.
Follow the rule: row by row. Say each number out loud as you "visit" it.
Write the numbers in the order you said them.
Try the other three orders on the same tree. Are the lists the same?
offline.think: Which order gives a sorted list on a search tree?

name: Lowest common ancestor
blurb: The lowest common ancestor of two nodes is the first node they both have above them. Lift the deeper node up until both are level, then lift both together until they meet.
code: while the two nodes are at different depths
lift the deeper one to its parent
while the two nodes differ
lift both to their parents
where they meet is the answer

offline.title: Family tree meeting
offline.need: A family tree drawn on paper
steps: Draw a tree of 9 people, parents above children.
Pick two people. Put a finger on each.
Move the finger on the lower person up until both fingers are on the same generation.
Move both fingers up one parent at a time until they land on the same person. That is the lowest common ancestor.
offline.think: Why does lifting the deeper node first make the climb together work?

name: Heaps and priority queues
blurb: A heap keeps the smallest number on top. A new number goes in at the bottom and swaps up while it is smaller than its parent. To take the smallest, remove the top and sink the last number down.
code: add: put the new number at the end
while it is smaller than its parent: swap up
remove: take the top
move the last number to the top
while it is bigger than a child: swap with the smaller child

offline.title: The family pyramid
offline.need: Number cards and a pyramid drawn on paper
steps: Draw a pyramid: 1 box on top, 2 below, 4 below those. Boxes are filled left to right.
Place each new card in the next empty box. If it is smaller than the card above it, swap them, and repeat.
After 7 cards, the smallest is on top. Take it. Put the last card on top and sink it by swapping with its smaller child.
The new top is the second smallest.
offline.think: Where in the pyramid can the third smallest number be?

name: Heap sort
blurb: Turn the row into a heap with the biggest on top. Swap the top with the last place: that number is finished. Fix the heap and repeat until every number is finished.
code: build a max-heap (biggest on top)
repeat:
swap the top with the last unfinished place
that place is now finished
sift the new top down to rebuild the heap

offline.title: Pyramid sort
offline.need: Number cards (7) and a pyramid drawn on paper
steps: Fill the pyramid with the cards, then fix it so every card is bigger than the cards below it.
Swap the top card with the last card in the pyramid. Set that card aside: it is the biggest.
Sink the new top card down until the pyramid is in order again.
Keep going. The cards you set aside, read backward, are sorted.
offline.think: Why is the biggest card always on top of a max-heap?

name: Tries
blurb: A trie stores words letter by letter along a path. Words that start the same share the same first steps. To find every word with a given start, walk down the prefix and collect everything below.
code: start at the root
for each letter of the word
follow that letter, or make a new branch
mark the last node as a word end
to search a prefix: follow its letters, then collect words below

offline.title: Autocomplete tree
offline.need: Paper and a pencil, and 4 short words
steps: Pick 4 words that share some starting letters, like CAT, CAR, COW, DOG.
Draw a dot at the top. For each word, follow or draw one branch per letter. Reuse a branch if it already exists.
Mark the end of each word with a circle.
Pick a prefix like CA. Walk down it and list every word you can reach below.
offline.think: How much work does it take to find all the words starting with CA when there are a million words?

name: Balanced trees (AVL)
blurb: A search tree is fast only if it stays bushy. Adding numbers in order makes a lopsided stick. An AVL tree checks each node, and when one side gets two levels taller than the other, it rotates to fix it.
code: add the number like a normal search tree
going back up, check each node: left height − right height
if it is 2 or −2, this node is lopsided
rotate it to even the sides out
the tree is balanced again

offline.title: Tip the tree
offline.need: Paper, a pencil and 6 numbers in increasing order
steps: Draw a search tree by adding 10, 20, 30 in that order. It is a stick leaning right.
The top node has nothing on its left but two levels on its right. Rotate: make 20 the top, with 10 on its left and 30 on its right.
Keep adding 40, 50, 60. Every time one side gets two levels taller than the other, rotate.
Count the height of your tree and compare with a plain stick of 6.
offline.think: Why is a stick of 1000 numbers so much slower to search than a balanced tree of 1000?

name: Segment trees
blurb: A segment tree keeps the sum of every chunk of a row: the whole row on top, halves below, single numbers at the bottom. Any stretch can be added up by combining just a few chunks.
code: leaves hold the numbers
each parent holds the sum of its two children
query(range): if a chunk is fully inside, use it
if it only partly overlaps, ask both children
if it is outside, skip it

offline.title: Sum pyramid
offline.need: Paper and 8 numbers
steps: Write 8 numbers in a row. Above each pair, write their sum. Above each pair of sums, write their sum. The top is the total.
Pick a stretch, like numbers 3 to 7. Find the biggest boxes that fit entirely inside it.
Add just those boxes. Check with a slow sum.
offline.think: How many boxes do you add for the stretch 1 to 7 of 8 numbers?

name: Fenwick trees
blurb: A Fenwick tree stores running totals in a clever way. Each cell adds up a block of numbers that ends there. A total of the first few numbers needs only a few cells.
code: T[i] = sum of the last (lowest set bit of i) numbers
prefix(k): total ← 0, i ← k
while i > 0:
total ← total + T[i]
i ← i − (lowest set bit of i)

offline.title: Binary jumps
offline.need: Paper and 8 numbers
steps: Write numbers at positions 1 to 8. Under position 4 write the sum of positions 1 to 4. Under position 6 write the sum of positions 5 and 6.
For position 7 you only need positions 5 to 7... find the pattern: the box under position i covers a block that ends at i, whose length is the biggest power of 2 dividing i.
To add up the first 7 numbers, add the boxes under 7, then 6, then 4.
Check with a slow sum.
offline.think: Why do you jump from 7 to 6 to 4?

name: Sparse tables
blurb: A sparse table writes down the smallest number in every block that is 1, 2, 4 or 8 long. Any stretch is covered by two blocks that overlap, so each question takes one look.
code: level 0: the numbers themselves
level k: min of two blocks of level k−1
query(l, r): k ← biggest power of 2 that fits
answer ← min(block at l, block ending at r)

offline.title: Overlapping blocks
offline.need: Paper and 8 numbers
steps: Write 8 numbers. Underneath, write the smaller of each neighbouring pair. Underneath that, the smallest of each 4 in a row.
To find the smallest in a stretch of 6, pick the biggest block that fits (4). Use one block at the start and one ending at the end. They overlap.
The smaller of those two block values is the answer.
offline.think: Why does the overlap not matter for "smallest"? Would it matter for "sum"?

name: B-trees
blurb: A B-tree keeps several numbers in each node, so the tree is short and wide. Databases love that. When a node gets too full it splits, and the middle number moves up.
code: walk down to the leaf where the number belongs
put the number in that leaf, in order
if the node now holds 3 numbers: split it
the middle number moves up to the parent
if the root splits, the tree grows taller

offline.title: Boxes of numbers
offline.need: Paper, a pencil and 7 numbers
steps: Draw a box that can hold at most 2 numbers. Add numbers in order into the right place.
When a box would hold 3, split it: the middle number goes up into a new box above, and the other two become its children.
Keep adding. Every time a box fills to 3, split it.
Check: are all the bottom boxes on the same level?
offline.think: Why does a B-tree never get lopsided the way a plain search tree can?

name: Skip lists
blurb: A skip list is a sorted list with express lanes. The top lane leaps far. Go right while the next number is not too big, then drop down a lane. It searches fast, like a tree, but it is only lists.
code: start at the top lane, left end
if the next number on this lane is not past the target: move right
otherwise: drop down one lane
on the bottom lane: stop at the target, or it is missing

offline.title: Express lanes
offline.need: Paper: a bottom row of 8 sorted numbers, and shorter rows above
steps: Write 8 sorted numbers on the bottom row. Copy about half of them to a row above, and about half of those to a row above that.
Pick a target. Start at the left of the top row and move right while the next number is not bigger than the target.
Drop down a row and keep moving right. Stop at the bottom row.
Count your moves, and compare with moving along the bottom row only.
offline.think: Why does the top lane help most when the target is far to the right?

name: Tree DP
blurb: Pick nodes in a tree to get the most total value, but never two nodes that are joined. For each node work out the best total if you take it and if you skip it, using what its children already found.
code: for each node, children first
take it: its value + each child's skip total
skip it: each child's better of take and skip
the answer is the bigger of the root's two totals

offline.title: Pick without neighbours
offline.need: A tree of 7 circles on paper, each with a value
steps: Draw a tree and write a value in each circle.
Work from the bottom up. Beside each circle write two numbers: best if I take it, best if I skip it.
Take = its value + the skip numbers of its children. Skip = the bigger of each child's two numbers, added up.
The bigger of the top circle's two numbers is your answer.
offline.think: Why can a child's answer be reused, instead of being worked out again?

name: Treaps
blurb: A treap is a search tree with a random priority on every node. Keys keep the order left to right. Priorities keep the biggest at the top. The randomness keeps the tree bushy, even when the keys arrive in order.
code: add the node like a normal search tree, by key
give it a random priority (p)
while its priority is higher than its parent's:
rotate it above its parent
search order and priority order both hold

offline.title: Keys and dice
offline.need: Paper, a pencil, a dice or number cards for priorities, and 7 numbers in order
steps: Write 7 numbers in increasing order. Give each a random priority (draw numbers from a hat).
Add them to a search tree one at a time by key. A plain tree would be a stick.
After adding a node, if its priority is bigger than its parent's, swap their places by rotating, and repeat.
Compare the height of your tree with a stick of 7.
offline.think: Why does random priority make the tree behave as if the keys had arrived in random order?

name: Heavy-light decomposition
blurb: Split a tree into long chains by always going down to the child with the biggest subtree. Any path then crosses only a few chains, because each time you leave a chain the tree at least doubles.
code: size[node] ← 1 + the sizes of its children
heavy child ← the child with the biggest size
a heavy child continues its parent's chain
every other child starts a new chain
path query: while the chains differ, jump the deeper chain's head to its parent

offline.title: Chains in a tree
offline.need: A tree of 9 circles on paper and coloured pencils
steps: Draw a tree of 9 circles. Write beside each circle the size of the tree hanging below it (itself included).
From each circle, draw a thick line to the child with the larger size. Thin lines go to the others.
Colour each chain of thick lines in one colour. Every circle belongs to exactly one chain.
Pick two circles. Count how many times a path between them switches colour.
offline.think: Why does the subtree at least double each time you take a thin line upward?

name: Graphs as pictures
blurb: A graph is dots (nodes) joined by lines (edges). To store one, write for every dot the list of its neighbours. Roads, friends and web links are all graphs.
code: for each dot, keep a list of neighbours
adding a line A–B: add B to A's list
and A to B's list
neighbours of a dot = its list

offline.title: Draw the web
offline.need: Paper and a pencil
steps: Draw 6 dots and name them A to F. Join some with lines.
Next to each dot, write the names of the dots it touches. That is its neighbour list.
Pick a dot and check: does each neighbour list it back?
Count the lines. Add up all the neighbour list lengths. What do you notice?
offline.think: Why is the total of all the list lengths exactly twice the number of lines?

name: Connected components
blurb: A graph can be split into separate islands. Start anywhere and colour everything you can reach. Then start again at a dot you have not reached. The number of fresh starts is the number of islands.
code: for each dot
if it is not reached yet:
a new island! explore it all
mark everything reached with this colour
count the fresh starts

offline.title: Count the islands
offline.need: A drawing of 9 dots and some lines, and 3 coloured pencils
steps: Draw 9 dots and join some. Leave some dots cut off from others.
Pick a dot and colour it. Then colour every dot you can reach by following lines.
Pick an uncoloured dot with a new colour and repeat.
The number of colours you used is the number of islands.
offline.think: Can two dots of different colours ever share a line?

name: Cycle detection in graphs
blurb: Walk the graph depth-first. If you meet a dot you have already visited, and it is not the one you just came from, you have found a way round: a cycle.
facts: A way back to the start
code: visit a dot, remember where we came from
for each neighbour
if it is the dot we came from: ignore
if it was already visited: a cycle!
else visit it
no repeat found: no cycle

offline.title: Find the loop
offline.need: A drawing of 6 dots and 5 or 6 lines, and a pencil
steps: Draw 6 dots joined by 5 lines so every dot is reachable. Walk from dot A, marking each dot you reach.
Add one more line between two dots that are already joined by a path.
Walk again. When a line leads to a marked dot (that you did not just come from), you have found the loop.
offline.think: Why does a connected graph with n dots and n − 1 lines never have a cycle?

name: Two-colouring (bipartite)
blurb: Can you colour the dots with two colours so every line joins different colours? Colour one dot, then give its neighbours the other colour, and keep going. If a line joins two of the same colour, it cannot be done.
code: colour the first dot green
take a dot from the queue
each neighbour gets the opposite colour
if a neighbour already has the same colour: impossible
every dot coloured: it works

offline.title: Two crayons
offline.need: A drawing of a loop of dots, and 2 crayons
steps: Draw a loop of 4 dots and join them in a ring. Colour one dot red.
Colour its neighbours blue, then their neighbours red, going round the ring.
Does it work? Now try a loop of 5.
offline.think: Why does an odd-length loop always fail?

name: Topological sort
blurb: Some jobs must wait for others. Count how many things each job is waiting for. Do any job that is waiting for nothing, then tell the jobs after it that one wait is over. Repeat.
code: count what each job is waiting for
queue every job waiting for nothing
take a job from the queue and do it
for each job after it: its count goes down by one
if a count reaches 0: add it to the queue
order done = a valid order

offline.title: Getting ready
offline.need: Cards for 6 jobs, and arrows drawn between them
steps: Write jobs on cards: Wake, Wash, Dress, Eat, Pack, Go. Draw an arrow from each job to one that must come after it.
Next to each card write how many arrows point into it.
Do a card with 0, write the order down, and cross out the arrows leaving it.
Repeat until all cards are done.
offline.think: Can there be more than one valid order? What if two jobs wait for each other?

name: Union-find
blurb: Keep groups as small trees. Each item points to a parent, and the top of a tree is the group's name. To join two groups, hang one top under the other.
code: find(x): follow parents until an item is its own parent
point everything on the way straight at the top
union(a, b): find both tops
if they differ, hang one under the other
same top = same group

offline.title: Friend circles
offline.need: 8 name cards and some string
steps: Give each person a card and make each their own group (a card pointing at itself).
To join two people: follow arrows from each up to their leader, then make one leader point at the other.
After several joins, ask: are these two in the same group? Follow arrows to the leaders and compare.
offline.think: Why is it worth pointing everyone straight at the leader after looking them up?

name: Bellman-Ford
blurb: Dijkstra needs every road to cost something. Bellman-Ford can handle a road that gives you a refund. It tries every road again and again, and keeps any shorter way it finds, until nothing changes.
code: start: 0 for Home, ∞ for every other town
repeat up to (towns − 1) times:
for every road u → v of length w:
if dist[u] + w < dist[v]: update dist[v]
if a whole round changes nothing: stop

offline.title: Try every road
offline.need: Paper, a pencil and a small map with one negative road
steps: Draw 5 towns and some one-way roads with lengths. Make one road a refund, like −2.
Write 0 by Home and ∞ by the others.
Go through every road in any order. If dist[start] + length beats dist[end], cross out and write the better number.
Go through all roads again. Stop when a whole pass changes nothing.
offline.think: Why can the answer never need more than (towns − 1) rounds?

name: All-pairs shortest paths (Floyd-Warshall)
blurb: Make a table of the shortest way between every pair of towns. Try each town as a stop-over, one at a time. If going through it is shorter, update the table.
code: table[i][j] ← direct road, or ∞
for each stop-over town k
for each pair i, j:
if table[i][k] + table[k][j] < table[i][j]:
table[i][j] ← that sum
table holds every shortest distance

offline.title: The distance table
offline.need: Paper (a 4 by 4 grid) and a small map
steps: Draw 4 towns with one-way roads. Fill a 4 by 4 table with the direct road lengths, ∞ where there is none, 0 on the diagonal.
Pick town A as the stop-over. For every cell, check: is (row to A) + (A to column) smaller? If so, write it in.
Repeat with B, then C, then D as the stop-over.
The table now holds the shortest distance between every pair.
offline.think: Why does the order of the stop-over towns not matter, as long as you use each once?

name: Minimum spanning trees
blurb: Join every town with the cheapest total road. Sort the roads from cheapest to dearest. Take a road only if it joins two towns that are not already connected, so it never makes a loop.
code: sort the roads, cheapest first
for each road
if its ends are in different groups:
take the road, join the groups
else skip it (it would make a loop)
total of the taken roads

offline.title: Cheapest network
offline.need: Paper, a pencil and a small map with road costs
steps: Draw 6 towns and 8 roads with different costs.
List the roads from cheapest to dearest.
Go down the list. Draw a road in colour only if it does not close a loop with roads already coloured.
Stop when all 6 towns are joined (5 roads). Add up the costs.
offline.think: Why is it safe to always take the cheapest road that does not close a loop?

name: A* search
blurb: Like breadth-first search, but it has a nose for the goal. Score each square by the steps so far plus a guess of the steps left. Always explore the square with the lowest score.
code: open ← [start]
take the open square with the smallest f = g + h
if it is the goal: stop
for each neighbour: g ← g + 1, f ← g + h
add it to the open list
follow the way back to draw the path

offline.title: Guided walk
offline.need: Squared paper, a pencil and a pair of coloured pencils
steps: Draw a 5 by 7 grid. Shade a few walls. Mark start (top left) and goal (bottom right).
For a square, g is the steps you have walked to reach it. h is the number of squares across plus down to the goal, ignoring walls.
Write f = g + h in each square you reach. Always continue from the open square with the smallest f.
When you reach the goal, trace the way back.
offline.think: Why does the guess h help, and what would happen if h were always 0?

name: Network flow
blurb: Pipes have limits. How much can flow from the start S to the end T? Find a route with room, push as much as fits, and repeat. When no route is left, you have found the most.
code: flow ← 0
find a route S → T where every pipe has spare room
push as much as the tightest pipe allows
add it to the flow; use up that room
no route left: the flow is the most possible

offline.title: Pipes and buckets
offline.need: Paper, a pencil and a drawing of 6 dots joined by arrows with limits
steps: Draw S, A, B, C, T with arrows and write a limit on each arrow.
Find a route from S to T. The most you can send is the smallest limit along it. Write that flow on each arrow and subtract it from the limits.
Find another route using the room that is left. Repeat until none exists.
Add up everything you sent.
offline.think: Why can the flow never be more than the total limit of the pipes leaving S?

name: Bipartite matching
blurb: Pair each person on the left with a different friend on the right, using only the allowed links. If their favourite is taken, ask the one holding it to switch. A chain of switches can make room.
code: for each person on the left
for each allowed partner on the right
if the partner is free: pair them
else ask their current partner to try someone else
if that works: pair them
count the pairs

offline.title: Dance partners
offline.need: 4 names on the left, 4 on the right, and lines for who may pair
steps: Draw 4 people on the left and 4 on the right. Draw lines for allowed pairs.
Take the left people in order. Pair each with the first allowed partner who is free.
If a left person has only taken partners, ask one of those partners' current pairs to switch to another allowed partner.
Count the pairs. Can you find a way to get more?
offline.think: Why does a chain of switches never leave anyone worse off?

name: Strongly connected components
blurb: On one-way roads, a strongly connected group is a set of towns where you can get from any town to any other. Search once to see which towns finish first. Then search the roads backwards, starting from the last one.
code: pass 1: depth-first search, note the order towns finish
reverse every road
pass 2: take towns in reverse finish order
search the reversed roads from it
everything reached is one group

offline.title: One-way streets
offline.need: Paper, a pencil and a drawing of 7 towns with one-way arrows
steps: Draw 7 towns and some one-way arrows.
Pass 1: walk depth-first from any town. Write each town down at the moment you have finished with it.
Redraw every arrow backward. Pass 2: take the town you wrote last. Walk along the backward arrows to everything you can reach that is not yet coloured. That is one group.
Repeat with the next-latest uncoloured town.
offline.think: Can two different groups ever reach each other in both directions?

name: Bridges and cut points
blurb: A bridge is a road that splits the network if you close it. Walk depth-first and note when you reach each town and the earliest town it can get back to. If a town cannot get back past its parent, the road to it is a bridge.
code: disc[u] ← the time we first reach u; low[u] ← disc[u]
for each road u – v (not the one we came by)
new town: search it, then low[u] ← min(low[u], low[v])
if low[v] > disc[u]: the road is a bridge
seen town: low[u] ← min(low[u], disc[v])

offline.title: Which road is a lifeline?
offline.need: A drawing of 7 towns and 8 roads, and a pencil
steps: Draw 7 towns joined by roads, with a couple of loops.
For each road, imagine closing it. Can you still get from any town to any other? If not, it is a bridge.
Notice that bridges are never part of a loop.
offline.think: Why can a road inside a loop never be a bridge?

name: Euler circuits
blurb: Can you walk along every road exactly once and end where you started? Yes, if every town has an even number of roads. Walk until you are stuck, then add in any loops you skipped.
code: check: every town has an even number of roads
walk along unused roads, noting each town
when stuck, back up and add that town to the finished route
keep going until nothing is left
the finished route (reversed) is the circuit

offline.title: Snow plough
offline.need: A drawing of a ring of 6 towns with three extra roads, and a pencil
steps: Draw 6 towns in a ring and add a triangle joining three of them. Count the roads at each town.
Start anywhere and trace every road once without lifting your pencil. If you get stuck, find a town on your route that still has unused roads and walk a loop from there.
You should finish where you began.
offline.think: What goes wrong if two towns have an odd number of roads? What if four do?

name: Hamilton paths
blurb: An Euler walk uses every road once. A Hamilton path visits every town once. It sounds similar but is much harder, and nobody knows a quick test. Try a path, and step back when you get stuck.
code: start in a town
go to a neighbour you have not visited
if every town is visited: found a Hamilton path
if stuck: step back and try another neighbour
tried every start: there is no Hamilton path

offline.title: Visit every town
offline.need: A drawing of 6 towns joined by roads, and a pencil
steps: Draw 6 towns in a ring and add a couple of extra roads.
Pick a start. Walk to a neighbour you have not visited, marking each town. Try to visit all 6 without repeating one.
If you get stuck, step back one town and try a different road.
Now draw a "star": one town joined to three others, and one more town hanging off two of those. Can you do it?
offline.think: Why can a town with only one road be in the middle of a Hamilton path? (Hint: it cannot.)

name: Divide and conquer
blurb: Split a big problem into two halves, solve each half the same way, then combine the answers. Here the problem is the best run of numbers in a row. It is in the left half, in the right half, or across the middle.
code: solve(range): if one number, that is the answer
split the range in the middle
best of the left half
best of the right half
best run straddling the middle
answer ← the biggest of the three

offline.title: Halve and combine
offline.need: Paper and 8 numbers, some negative
steps: Write 8 numbers, some below zero. We want the biggest total of numbers next to each other.
Split into two halves of 4. Find the best run in each half the same way (split again until one number).
Now find the best run that crosses the middle: the best run ending at the middle, plus the best run starting after it.
The answer is the biggest of the three.
offline.think: Why do you need the crossing case? What would you miss without it?

name: Greedy choices
blurb: A greedy method always takes the best-looking choice right now and never looks back. Giving change with the biggest coins first works for many coins. But with some coins it gives a worse answer.
code: coins taken ← none; left ← the amount
repeat while something is left:
take the biggest coin that fits
subtract it from what is left
count the coins; compare with the best possible

offline.title: Change maker
offline.need: Coins or paper discs worth 25, 10, 5 and 1 (or 4, 3 and 1)
steps: Pick an amount, like 63. Always take the biggest coin that still fits.
Count your coins.
Now try coins worth 4, 3 and 1 for the amount 6. Greedy takes 4 + 1 + 1. Can you do it with fewer?
offline.think: For which coins does "biggest first" always give the fewest coins?

name: Interval scheduling
blurb: Many meetings want one room. To fit the most, sort them by when they end. Take the first, then the next one that starts after the last one ended. Finishing early leaves the most room.
code: sort meetings by finish time
chosen ← none; last end ← 0
for each meeting in order
if it starts after the last end: choose it
else skip it

offline.title: Fit the meetings
offline.need: Paper strips of different lengths and a long line marked 1 to 12
steps: Cut 7 strips and place each along the line where a meeting would run.
Sort the strips by where they end.
Take the first. Then take the next that begins after the last one chosen ends. Skip any that overlap.
Count the meetings you fit.
offline.think: Why sort by the end time and not by the start time or length?

name: Backtracking
blurb: Try a choice. If it leads nowhere, undo it and try another. For each number, take it or leave it. As soon as the total goes over the target, give up on that branch.
code: for each number, in order:
try taking it
if the total is over the target: give up (backtrack)
if the total equals the target: found!
then try leaving it out
every choice tried: no answer

offline.title: Pick and undo
offline.need: Paper, a pencil and 5 number cards
steps: Pick a target. Lay out 5 cards. Find cards that add exactly to the target.
Go card by card: take it (add it up) or leave it.
If your total goes over the target, stop and undo the last card you took. Try leaving it out instead.
Write down each take and undo so you can see the search.
offline.think: Why does giving up early on a bad branch save so much work?

name: N-Queens
blurb: Place queens on a board so none can capture another. Put one queen in each row. If a row has no safe square, go back to the row above and move its queen.
code: for each row
for each column: is it safe?
safe: place a queen, go to the next row
no safe column: go back and move the queen above
every row has a queen: solved

offline.title: Queens on paper
offline.need: A 5 by 5 grid on paper, and 5 coins
steps: Place a coin in the top row. A queen attacks along its row, column and both diagonals.
In the next row, put a coin on the first square no coin attacks.
If a row has no safe square, pick up the last coin and move it one square along. This is backtracking.
Continue until each row has a coin.
offline.think: How does moving back one row cut out thousands of silly positions at once?

name: Knapsack
blurb: A bag can only hold so much weight. Which items give the most value? Fill a table. For each item, either leave it, or take it and add its value to the best for the room that is left.
code: table[0][size] ← 0 (no items, no value)
for each item i, each bag size s
leave it: table[i−1][s]
take it (if it fits): value + table[i−1][s − weight]
table[i][s] ← the bigger of the two
the answer is the last cell

offline.title: Pack the bag
offline.need: Paper, a pencil and 4 items with weights and values
steps: Pick 4 items, each with a weight (1 to 5) and a value. The bag holds weight 8.
Draw a table: a row for each item added so far, a column for each bag size from 0 to 8.
Fill row by row. For each cell compare "leave the item" (the cell above) and "take it" (its value plus the cell above and to the left by its weight).
The last cell is the best value.
offline.think: Why does each cell only need to look at the row above?

name: Longest common subsequence
blurb: Two words can share letters in the same order, even if the letters are not side by side. Fill a table. If two letters match, add 1 to the cell up-left. If not, copy the bigger of the cell above and the cell to the left.
code: table[0][·] and table[·][0] are 0
for each letter pair (i, j)
if the letters match: table[i][j] ← table[i−1][j−1] + 1
else: table[i][j] ← the bigger of the cell above and the cell to the left
the last cell is the length

offline.title: Shared letters
offline.need: Two short words on paper and a grid
steps: Write one word across the top and one down the side of a grid. Fill the first row and column with 0.
For each cell: if the two letters match, write one more than the cell up and to the left.
If not, write the bigger of the cell above and the cell to the left.
The bottom-right number is the length of the longest shared sequence.
offline.think: Is a shared sequence allowed to skip letters? Is it allowed to reorder them?

name: Longest increasing subsequence
blurb: Pick numbers from a row, left to right, so each one is bigger than the last. For each number, its best chain is 1 more than the best chain that ends at a smaller number before it.
code: best[i] ← 1 for every number
for each number i, left to right
for each earlier number j with a[j] < a[i]
best[i] ← the bigger of best[i] and best[j] + 1
the answer is the biggest best[i]

offline.title: Climbing the row
offline.need: Paper and 8 numbers in a row
steps: Write 8 numbers. Under each, write 1.
Go left to right. For each number look at the numbers before it that are smaller.
Under this number write one more than the biggest number under those smaller ones.
The biggest number written is the length of the longest climb.
offline.think: Why does a number's answer only depend on numbers to its left?

name: Edit distance
blurb: How many edits turn one word into another? An edit is adding, removing or changing one letter. A table stores the cheapest way to turn each start of one word into each start of the other.
code: table[i][0] ← i; table[0][j] ← j
for each letter pair (i, j)
if the letters match: copy the cell up-left
else: 1 + the smallest of up, left and up-left
the last cell is the distance

offline.title: Fix the word
offline.need: Two short words, paper and a pencil
steps: Pick two words like CAT and CUT. Draw a grid with a blank row and column first.
The first row counts 0, 1, 2, … and so does the first column.
Each cell: if the letters match, copy the cell up and to the left. If not, add 1 to the smallest of the cell above, the cell to the left and the cell up-left.
The last cell is the fewest edits.
offline.think: Why does the distance never exceed the length of the longer word?

name: Bit tricks: counting 1s
blurb: Computers store numbers as bits. Subtracting 1 flips the last 1 bit to 0. So n AND (n minus 1) removes exactly one 1 bit. Count how many times until you reach 0.
code: count ← 0
while n is not 0
n ← n AND (n − 1)  (removes the lowest 1)
count ← count + 1
count is the number of 1-bits

offline.title: Flip the last 1
offline.need: Paper and a pencil
steps: Write a number in binary, like 10110100.
Subtract 1 in binary. Notice the lowest 1 becomes 0 and the zeros after it become 1s.
Line up the old and new numbers and keep a 1 only where both have a 1 (AND). The lowest 1 has vanished.
Repeat until you reach 0. Count the repeats.
offline.think: Why does this loop run once per 1-bit and not once per bit?

name: Bit tricks: XOR
blurb: XOR gives 1 only where two bits are different, and a number XOR itself is 0. If every number appears twice except one, XOR them all. The pairs cancel and the loner is left.
code: answer ← 0
for each number n
answer ← answer XOR n
pairs cancel to 0, so answer is the number with no partner

offline.title: Cancelling pairs
offline.need: Paper and 7 numbers (3 pairs and 1 single)
steps: Write 7 numbers from 1 to 15: three numbers twice, and one number once. Shuffle them.
Write each in 4 bits. Start with 0000.
XOR each number in: where the bits differ, the result bit is 1.
When you finish, the pairs have cancelled and the single number is left.
offline.think: Why does the order of the numbers not matter?

name: Bitmask DP
blurb: A bitmask is a row of 0s and 1s that shows which jobs are taken. Store the cheapest cost for every mask. Build each answer from a smaller mask plus one more job.
code: best[000] ← 0 (no jobs taken)
for each mask, smallest first
worker ← the number of jobs taken
for each job j in the mask: best[mask without j] + cost[worker][j]
best[mask] ← the smallest of those
the answer is best[111]

offline.title: Jobs and workers
offline.need: A 3 by 3 table of costs, paper and a pencil
steps: Write a 3 by 3 table: the cost of each worker doing each job.
List all 8 subsets of jobs as 000, 001, … 111 (1 means the job is taken).
For each subset, the number of 1s tells you how many workers are done. Try removing each job in turn: previous best + that cost for the next worker. Keep the smallest.
The cost for 111 is the cheapest way to give every worker a different job.
offline.think: How many ways are there to give 20 workers 20 different jobs? How many masks are there?

name: Meet in the middle
blurb: Trying every subset of 8 numbers means 256 sets. Instead split the numbers in half. List the sums of each half, sort them, and use two pointers to find a pair that adds up to the target.
code: split the numbers into a left half and a right half
list every subset sum of each half; sort both lists
left pointer at the smallest left sum, right pointer at the biggest right sum
if the two add to the target: found
if too small move the left pointer up; if too big move the right pointer down

offline.title: Halve the search
offline.need: Paper and 6 numbers
steps: Write 6 numbers and a target. Split them into two groups of 3.
For each group, list all 8 subset sums (including the empty set, 0). Sort each list.
Put a finger at the start of the left list and another at the end of the right list. Add the two. Too small: move the left finger right. Too big: move the right finger left.
If the fingers add to the target, you have found a subset.
offline.think: For 40 numbers, how many sets would you try one by one? How many sums per half here?

name: Sudoku
blurb: Fill a 4 by 4 grid so every row, column and 2 by 2 box has 1 to 4 once. Try a digit in each empty square. If a square has nothing that fits, go back and change the last digit.
facts: No repeats in row, column or box
code: find the next empty square
for each digit 1 to 4: does it break a rule?
fits: write it, go on to the next empty square
nothing fits: go back and change the last digit
no empty squares: solved

offline.title: Mini sudoku
offline.need: A 4 by 4 grid on paper with a few digits filled in, and a pencil
steps: Draw a 4 by 4 grid in four 2 by 2 boxes and fill in a few digits.
Go to the first empty square. Write the smallest digit that does not repeat in its row, column or box (lightly, in pencil).
Move to the next. If no digit fits, rub out your last digit and try the next one up.
Continue until the grid is full.
offline.think: Why does rubbing out one digit fix many mistakes at once?

name: Pattern matching
blurb: To find a short word inside a long text, slide the word along one place at a time. At each place, compare letter by letter and stop at the first mismatch.
code: for each starting place in the text
compare the word with the text, letter by letter
if a letter differs: slide on
if every letter matches: found here
no more places to try

offline.title: Slide the word
offline.need: A strip of paper with a short word, and a longer text on paper
steps: Write a text of 12 letters from A, B and C. Write a pattern of 3 letters on a paper strip.
Place the strip under the start of the text. Do all three letters match? Tick or cross.
Slide the strip one place right and repeat until the end.
Mark every place where all three letters matched.
offline.think: How many comparisons would you need to find a 100-letter pattern in a million-letter text, if every place nearly matched?

name: Rolling hash (Rabin-Karp)
blurb: Give every stretch of text a fingerprint number and compare fingerprints first. Only when two fingerprints match, check the letters. Sliding along is cheap: drop the old digit, add the new one.
code: fingerprint of the word
fingerprint of the first stretch of text
for each stretch
if the fingerprints match: check the letters
slide: drop the old digit, add the new one
report every real match

offline.title: Fingerprints
offline.need: Digits on paper (a text of 12 digits) and a 3-digit word
steps: Write 12 digits. Pick a 3-digit pattern. Its fingerprint is its value divided by 97, remainder.
Find the fingerprint of the first 3 digits of the text the same way.
To slide one place: take away the old first digit's part (digit × 100), multiply by 10, add the new digit, and take the remainder again.
Only when two fingerprints are equal, compare the digits.
offline.think: Two different stretches can have the same fingerprint. Why do you still check the digits?

name: KMP (prefix table)
blurb: When a letter does not match, you already know the letters before it matched. A table made from the word tells you how far back to restart, so you never move back in the text.
code: table[i] ← length of the longest start of the word that is also an end of its first i+1 letters
for each letter of the text
while the word letter differs: fall back using the table
if it matches: move on in the word
if the whole word matched: found

offline.title: Slide smartly
offline.need: A paper strip with the word ABAB, and a text of 12 letters from A and B
steps: Build the table for ABAB. Position 3 (AB) is 0, position 3 (ABA) is 1 because A starts and ends it, position 4 (ABAB) is 2 (AB).
Match the word along the text. When a mismatch happens, do not slide back: restart in the word at the table value.
Mark every place where the word fully matches.
offline.think: Why can the text pointer never move backward?

name: Z-algorithm
blurb: For each place in a word, the Z-number says how many letters from there match the start of the word. Remembering the longest match so far saves comparing the same letters again.
code: Z[0] ← the whole word (skip it)
keep the window [l, r] of the furthest match
for each position i
inside the window: start from a known value
extend by comparing letters
grow the window if we passed r

offline.title: How much matches the start?
offline.need: A short word on paper
steps: Write the word AABXAAB. For each position, count how many letters in a row match the beginning of the word.
Position 2 (A) matches AAB... count it.
Write all the counts in a row. That is the Z row.
offline.think: What does a Z-value equal to the length of the pattern tell you if you search "pattern + # + text"?

name: Suffix arrays
blurb: Write every ending of a word and sort them like a dictionary. Words that start the same end up next to each other, so you can find them fast.
code: list every suffix of the word
sort the suffixes alphabetically
to find a pattern: binary search the sorted list
compare the pattern with the start of the middle suffix
all suffixes starting with the pattern are the matches

offline.title: Sorted endings
offline.need: A short word like BANANA, paper and a pencil
steps: Write BANANA. Underneath write each ending: BANANA, ANANA, NANA, ANA, NA, A. Number them by where they start.
Sort them like a dictionary: A, ANA, ANANA, BANANA, NA, NANA.
To find ANA, look in the sorted list. All the endings that start with ANA are next to each other.
The numbers beside them are where ANA occurs.
offline.think: Why are all the endings that start with the same pattern next to each other?

name: Compression (Huffman)
blurb: Give common letters short codes and rare letters long ones. Keep joining the two rarest items into one. The joins form a tree, and the path to each letter is its code of 0s and 1s.
code: put every letter in the queue with its count
take the two smallest items
join them into one item (add their counts)
put it back; repeat until one item is left
left branch = 0, right branch = 1

offline.title: Make a code
offline.need: Paper, a pencil and a short message
steps: Write a short message and count each letter.
Write each letter with its count. Cross out the two smallest and replace them with one item that has their total.
Repeat until one item is left. You have drawn a tree.
Label left branches 0 and right branches 1. Each letter's code is the path from the top to it.
offline.think: Why does giving the common letters shorter codes make the whole message shorter?

name: Bloom filters
blurb: A Bloom filter remembers words using a tiny row of bits. Each word switches on three bits. If any of a word's bits is off, it was definitely not added. If all are on, it was probably added.
code: start with 16 bits, all 0
add: switch on the 3 bits the word points to
ask: look at the word's 3 bits
any bit is 0: definitely not added
all bits 1: probably added

offline.title: Bit board
offline.need: 16 small squares on paper (or coins), and some words
steps: Draw a row of 16 boxes, all empty. Make up a rule that gives each word three box numbers (like adding letter positions).
To add a word, fill its three boxes.
To ask about a new word, look at its three boxes. Any empty box means it was never added.
If all three are filled you can only say "probably".
offline.think: Can a Bloom filter ever say "no" about a word that was added? Why not?

name: Count-min sketch
blurb: Count how often things appear in a huge stream using a small table. Each item adds 1 to one counter in each of three rows. To ask for a count, take the smallest of its three counters.
code: three rows of counters, all 0
for each item in the stream
add 1 to one counter in each row
to ask: look at its three counters
answer ← the smallest

offline.title: Tally boards
offline.need: Three rows of 6 boxes on paper and a stream of letters
steps: Draw three rows of 6 boxes. Make a rule for each row that sends a letter to one of its 6 boxes.
For each letter in a stream, add a tally in its box in every row.
To ask about a letter, look at its three boxes and take the smallest.
Compare with a true count. Is the answer ever lower?
offline.think: Why is the smallest of the three counters the best guess?

name: Caches (LRU)
blurb: A cache is a small, fast shelf for things you use a lot. When it is full, throw out the thing you used longest ago. Every time you use something, move it to the front.
code: cache holds 3 items, ordered by last use
item asked for:
in the cache (a hit): move it to the newest end
not there (a miss): fetch it
if full: remove the oldest
add it at the newest end

offline.title: The small desk
offline.need: 3 spaces on a desk, and cards A to D
steps: A desk fits only 3 cards. Someone asks for cards in a list like A B C A D B.
If the card is on the desk, slide it to the newest end. If not, fetch it. If the desk is full, send away the card that has been there untouched the longest.
Count hits (already on the desk) and misses.
offline.think: Why is "least recently used" a good guess for what you will not need next?

name: Counting with hashes
blurb: A hash map is like a notebook where you find things by name straight away. Look up each letter and add 1 to its tally. Then the first letter with a tally of 1 is the first that never repeats.
code: counts ← an empty hash map
for each letter: counts[letter] ← counts[letter] + 1
for each letter in order
if counts[letter] is 1: that is the answer
every letter repeats: no answer

offline.title: Tally the letters
offline.need: A word on paper and a pencil
steps: Write a word like SWISS... a longer one, like LETTERS.
Make a list of letters and a tally column. For each letter in the word, find its row and add a tally.
Now read the word again from the start. The first letter with a tally of 1 is the first letter that never repeats.
offline.think: Why is it better to keep a tally than to count the letter again every time you meet it?

name: HyperLogLog
blurb: How many different things went past? Scramble each one into bits and count the zeros at the start. Seeing a long run of zeros is rare, so a long run means a big crowd. One small counter gives a rough answer.
code: best ← 0
for each item: scramble it into 8 bits
count the zeros at the start
best ← the larger of best and that count
estimate ← 2 to the power (best + 1)

offline.title: Rare coin runs
offline.need: A coin
steps: Flip a coin until you get heads. Count the tails first (these are like leading zeros). Do it 8 times and write the biggest count.
Now do it 32 times. Does the biggest count go up?
The more people flipping, the longer the longest run. So the longest run tells you roughly how many flipped.
offline.think: Why does one very rare value suggest a big crowd rather than a lucky few?

name: Aho-Corasick
blurb: Search a text for many words at once. Build a trie of the words and give each node a fall-back link. Then read the text one time and never go back.
code: build a trie of all the words
fail link of a node ← the longest shorter ending that is also a start in the trie
for each letter of the text
while no branch for the letter: follow the fail link
step along the branch, then report every word that ends here (following fail links)

offline.title: Many words, one pass
offline.need: Paper, a pencil, a few short words and a text
steps: Draw a trie for the words HE, SHE, HIS and HERS.
For each node, work out where to fall back to if the next letter fails: the longest ending of what you have matched that is also a start of some word.
Read the text USHERS one letter at a time, moving along the trie or falling back.
Every time you reach a node where a word ends (or a fall-back chain through one), note the word.
offline.think: Why does reading "SHE" also find "HE"?

name: Modular arithmetic
blurb: Clock arithmetic: numbers wrap around. On a 12-hour clock, 9 o'clock plus 5 hours is 2 o'clock. "Mod 12" means: keep only the remainder after dividing by 12. Computers use it to keep numbers small.
code: start at a on a clock with m numbers (0 to m − 1)
move forward b steps, one at a time
past m − 1? wrap round to 0
where you stop is (a + b) mod m

offline.title: Be a clock
offline.need: A paper clock with the numbers 0 to 6 (or 0 to 11)
steps: Draw a clock with the numbers 0 to 6 round the edge.
Put a coin on 5. Move it forward 4 steps, one number at a time, wrapping from 6 to 0.
Where did it land? Check: (5 + 4) divided by 7, remainder.
Try a few more sums.
offline.think: What is 100 hours after 3 o'clock on a 12-hour clock?

name: Fast powers
blurb: You do not need 12 multiplications to work out 3 to the power 13. Write the power in binary. Square your answer for every bit, and also multiply by 3 when the bit is 1.
code: result ← 1
for each bit of the power, from the left
square the result (keep the remainder)
if the bit is 1: multiply by the base
result is base^power

offline.title: Square and multiply
offline.need: Paper and a calculator (optional)
steps: Write 13 in binary: 1101.
Start with 1. For the first bit (1): square, then multiply by 3. That gives 3.
Next bit (1): square → 9, multiply by 3 → 27. Next bit (0): just square → 729. Last bit (1): square, then multiply by 3.
Count the multiplications and compare with 12.
offline.think: How many multiplications does a power of one million need this way?

name: Counting (nCr)
blurb: How many ways can you choose 2 friends from 5? Pascal's triangle answers it. Each number is the sum of the two above it. The number in row n, place k is "n choose k".
code: row 0 is just 1
each row starts and ends with 1
every other number ← the number above-left + above
n choose k is the number in row n, place k

offline.title: Build the triangle
offline.need: Paper and a pencil
steps: Write 1 at the top. Below it write 1 1. Then 1 2 1. Each new row starts and ends with 1.
Each number in the middle is the two numbers above it added up.
Go to row 5 and read place 2: that is the number of ways to pick 2 things from 5.
Check by listing the pairs from A, B, C, D, E.
offline.think: Why does choosing 2 from 5 give the same number as choosing 3 from 5?

name: Chinese remainder theorem
blurb: Say a number leaves remainder 2 when divided by 3, and remainder 3 when divided by 5. Mark the numbers that fit the first clue, then the second. The number in both lists is the answer.
code: list the numbers 0 up to the product of the moduli − 1
mark those with the first remainder
mark those with the second remainder
the number marked twice is the answer

offline.title: Two clues
offline.need: A number line from 0 to 14 on paper, and two coloured pencils
steps: Draw the numbers 0 to 14.
Clue 1: the number leaves remainder 2 when divided by 3. Colour all numbers that do (2, 5, 8, 11, 14).
Clue 2: remainder 3 when divided by 5. Colour with the other pencil (3, 8, 13).
The number with both colours is the answer.
offline.think: Why do the clues pick out exactly one number below 15?

name: Randomised algorithms
blurb: Sometimes luck can answer a hard question. Throw darts at a square with a quarter-circle in it. The share that land inside tells you about the circle, and so about the number pi.
code: inside ← 0
throw a dart at a random square
if it lands inside the quarter-circle: inside ← inside + 1
after n darts: π ≈ 4 × inside ÷ n

offline.title: Dart board
offline.need: Squared paper (10 by 10), a dice or coin to choose squares, and a ruler
steps: Draw a 10 by 10 grid and a quarter-circle of radius 10 from the bottom-left corner.
Pick 20 random squares (roll a 10-sided dice twice, or draw numbers from a hat). Mark each one.
Count how many fall inside the curve.
Multiply that count by 4 and divide by 20. How close to 3.14 is it?
offline.think: What happens to your answer if you throw 1000 darts instead of 20?

name: Game theory (minimax)
blurb: Two players take turns removing 1, 2 or 3 stones. Whoever takes the last stone wins. Work backwards: a pile is a win if one move leaves your opponent a losing pile.
code: a pile of 0: the player to move has lost
for each pile size n, smallest first
look at the piles after taking 1, 2 or 3
if any of them is a loss for the opponent: n is a win
else n is a loss

offline.title: Play the stones
offline.need: 13 coins or counters and a friend
steps: Put 13 coins in a pile. Take turns removing 1, 2 or 3. Whoever takes the last coin wins.
Play a few games. Try to find a pile size that is always bad for whoever is about to move.
Work out why multiples of 4 are the losing piles: whatever you take, your friend can take enough to leave another multiple of 4.
offline.think: If you go first with 13 coins, how many should you take?

name: Easy and hard problems (P vs NP)
blurb: Some problems are quick to check but seem slow to solve. Checking a guess takes one pass. Finding an answer may mean trying every set, and the number of sets doubles with each new number.
code: to check a guess: add it up, compare with the target
to find one: try every set
with n numbers there are 2ⁿ sets
each new number doubles the work

offline.title: Doubling sets
offline.need: Paper and a pencil
steps: List all the sets you can make from the numbers {1}: there are 2 (empty, and {1}).
Now from {1, 2}: 4 sets. From {1, 2, 3}: 8. List them all.
Check a guess like {1, 3} with one addition. How many sets would you list for 20 numbers?
offline.think: If a computer could check a billion sets a second, how long would 60 numbers take?

topic: Easy and hard problems (P vs NP)

name: Approximation
blurb: Some problems are too hard to solve perfectly in time. A good guess that is fast and never too far off is useful. Guard roads by putting guards at both ends of an unguarded road. You never use more than twice the best.
code: guards ← none
pick any road with no guard at either end
put guards at both ends
now every road touching those towns is guarded
repeat until every road is guarded

offline.title: Guard the roads
offline.need: Paper and a pencil, and a small map of 6 towns and 7 roads
steps: Draw 6 towns and 7 roads. A guard in a town protects every road that touches it.
Pick any unguarded road. Put guards at both its ends. Cross out every road they now protect.
Repeat until all roads are crossed out. Count the guards.
Try to find a smaller set by thinking. Is yours less than half of what the quick method used?
offline.think: Why can the best possible answer never use fewer than half as many guards as this quick method?

name: Convex hull
blurb: Stretch a rubber band around some points. The points it touches make the convex hull. Walk the points from left to right, and whenever a point sticks inwards, drop it.
facts: Which way do three points turn?
code: sort the points from left to right
build the lower chain: add each point
while the last three turn the wrong way: drop the middle one
build the upper chain the same way, right to left
join the two chains

offline.title: Rubber band
offline.need: A board, 8 pins or coins, and a loop of string or a rubber band
steps: Place 8 pins on a board in a scatter.
Stretch the band around all of them and let it settle.
The pins the band touches are the hull. Write down their order going round.
Try moving one pin inside the band. Does the hull change?
offline.think: Can a point in the middle ever be on the hull?

name: Line sweep
blurb: Sweep an invisible line across time and stop only when a meeting starts or ends. Add 1 at a start, take away 1 at an end, and remember the biggest number. That is how many meetings overlap.
code: list every start (+1) and end (−1) as an event
sort the events by time (ends before starts at a tie)
sweep through the events
add its +1 or −1 to the running count
remember the biggest count

offline.title: Sweep the timeline
offline.need: Paper strips marking meetings on a timeline from 0 to 12
steps: Draw 6 meetings as bars along a timeline.
Write a + at each start and a − at each end, in order along the timeline.
Walk along the line keeping a count: add 1 at a +, subtract 1 at a −.
The biggest count is the number of rooms you need.
offline.think: Why can you ignore all the times when nothing starts or ends?

name: Closest pair of points
blurb: Which two points are nearest? Checking every pair is slow. Sort the points left to right. For each point, only look at points to its right, and stop when the sideways gap is already bigger than the best distance.
facts: Stop when the x-gap is too big
code: sort the points by x
best ← the distance of the first pair
for each point i
look at later points j
stop if the x-gap is already at least best
update best if the pair is closer

offline.title: Nearest neighbours
offline.need: Squared paper with 7 dots
steps: Draw 7 dots on squared paper. Number them left to right.
Start with dot 1 and dot 2 as your best pair. Measure the gap.
For each dot, check the dots to its right. Stop looking as soon as a dot is further away sideways than your best gap.
Mark the closest pair.
offline.think: Why can you stop looking once the sideways gap is as big as the best distance?

name: Bubble sort
blurb: Walk along the list and swap any two neighbours that are in the wrong order. Each walk carries the biggest number left to the end, like a bubble rising.
code: for each pass i = 0, 1, …
swapped ← false
for j = 0 … n−2−i
if a[j] > a[j+1]
swap a[j], a[j+1]; swapped ← true
a[n−1−i] is in place
if not swapped: stop

offline.title: The bubble line-up
offline.need: 4 to 8 people, or 8 playing cards
steps: Stand in a line in any order.
Start at the left end. Look at the first two people. If the taller one is on the left, they swap places.
Take one step right and check the next two. Keep going to the end of the line.
The tallest person is now at the right end. They are sorted, so they can sit down.
Start again from the left. You are done when you walk the whole line and nobody swaps.
offline.think: How many times did the shortest person move? Why do small values travel left so slowly?

name: Selection sort
blurb: Look through the unsorted numbers, find the smallest, and move it to the front. Then do it again with what is left.
code: for i = 0 … n−2
min ← i
for j = i+1 … n−1
if a[j] < a[min]: min ← j
swap a[i], a[min]
a[i] is in place

offline.title: Find the smallest
offline.need: 8 playing cards (ace counts as 1)
steps: Lay the cards face up in a row, all mixed up.
Touch each card one at a time and find the smallest.
Move it down to start a new row underneath.
Do the same with the cards that are left, until the top row is empty.
offline.think: Count every card you touch. With 8 cards it is always 28, however they start. Can you work out why?

name: Insertion sort
