blurb: Keep a sorted part on the left. Take the next number and slide it left until it fits, the way most people sort a hand of cards.
code: for i = 1 … n−1
key ← a[i]
while left neighbour > key
shift neighbour right; key moves left
key is placed

offline.title: Sort your hand
offline.need: 8 playing cards, face down in a pile
steps: Pick up one card. A hand of one card is already sorted.
Pick up the next card and slide it into the right place in your hand.
Keep going, one card at a time, until the pile is gone.
Now deal the cards out already in order and do it again. Notice how much faster it is.
offline.think: Why does insertion sort get so quick when the cards are nearly in order already?

name: Merge sort
blurb: Split the list in half again and again until every piece has one number. Then merge the pieces back together in order.
code: mergeSort(lo, hi)
if lo ≥ hi: return
mid ← ⌊(lo + hi) / 2⌋
mergeSort(lo, mid); mergeSort(mid+1, hi)
while both halves have items
write the smaller front item
copy any leftovers

offline.title: Split and merge
offline.need: 8 playing cards and a table
steps: Split the cards into 2 piles of 4. Split those into 4 piles of 2. Split again into 8 single cards.
Merge the single cards in pairs, smaller card on top.
Merge two pairs into a sorted pile of 4. Only look at the top card of each pile and take the smaller one.
Merge the two piles of 4 into one sorted pile of 8.
offline.think: When you merge, you only ever compare the top two cards. Why is that enough?

name: Quick sort
blurb: Pick one number as the pivot. Put everything smaller on its left, and the pivot lands in its final spot. Then do the same on each side.
code: quickSort(lo, hi)
if lo ≥ hi: return
pivot ← a[hi]; i ← lo
for j = lo … hi−1
if a[j] < pivot: swap a[i], a[j]; i ← i+1
swap a[i], a[hi]    // pivot placed
quickSort(lo, i−1); quickSort(i+1, hi)

offline.title: The pivot game
offline.need: 8 to 10 playing cards
steps: Mix the cards and pick the last one as the pivot. Put it in the middle of the table.
Every card smaller than the pivot goes in a pile on its left. Every other card goes on its right.
The pivot is now in its final place. Leave it there.
Play the same game with the left pile, then the right pile, until every pile has one card.
offline.think: What happens if the pivot is always the biggest card? Try it, and count how many times you compare.

name: Linear search
blurb: Open the boxes one by one, from the first to the last, until you find the number. Simple, and it works even when the boxes are in no order at all.
code: for i = 1 … n
open box i
if it is the target: found!
the target is not here

offline.title: Find the ace
offline.need: 10 playing cards with one ace, and a friend
steps: Your friend shuffles the cards and lays them face down in a row.
Turn over the cards one at a time, starting from the left.
Make a tally mark for every card you turn. Stop when you find the ace.
Swap roles and play five rounds. Write down how many cards you turned each time.
offline.think: What is the most cards you could ever turn? What is the average? What would it be with a whole deck of 52?

name: Binary search
blurb: When the boxes are in order, open the middle one. If your number is bigger it must be on the right, and if smaller, on the left. Each box you open throws away half of what is left.
code: lo ← first box; hi ← last box
while lo ≤ hi
open the middle box, mid
if it is the target: found!
if it is smaller: lo ← mid + 1
else: hi ← mid − 1
the target is not here

offline.title: Guess my number
offline.need: Two people. Nothing else.
steps: One person thinks of a whole number from 1 to 100 and keeps it secret.
The other person guesses. The answer is only ever "higher", "lower" or "yes!".
Always guess the middle of what is left. Start with 50. If the answer is "higher", the next guess is 75.
Count the guesses. Then swap roles.
offline.think: Seven guesses are always enough for 1 to 100. How many would you need for 1 to 1,000? For every person on Earth?

name: Breadth-first search
blurb: Keep a queue of squares to visit, like the line at a shop. Always take the square that has waited longest. The search spreads out like ripples, so the first route it finds is the shortest.
code: queue ← [home]
while the queue is not empty
square ← take from the FRONT
if square is school: stop
for each new open neighbour
mark it seen; add to BACK
follow the arrows back home

offline.title: Ripple map
offline.need: Squared paper and a pencil
steps: Draw a map on squared paper. Shade some squares as walls. Mark one square as home and one as school.
Write 0 in the home square.
Write 1 in every open square touching the 0. Then write 2 in every empty open square touching a 1, and so on, like ripples in a pond.
Stop when you write a number in the school square. That number is the length of the shortest walk.
Walk back from school, always stepping to a number one smaller, and draw the route.
offline.think: Why can there never be a shorter walk than the number you wrote in the school square?

name: Depth-first search
blurb: Keep a stack of squares to visit, like a pile of plates. Always take the newest one off the top. The search dives down one path as far as it can, then backs up. It finds a route, but not always the shortest.
code: stack ← [home]
while the stack is not empty
square ← take from the TOP
if square is school: stop
for each new open neighbour
mark it seen; put on TOP
follow the arrows back home

offline.title: Explore and back up
offline.need: A maze drawn on paper, and a few coins
steps: Draw a maze, or ask someone to draw one for you. Put your finger on the start.
Each time you reach a fork, put a coin on it, then take a way you have not tried.
At a dead end, go back to the last coin you put down and try another way from there.
When every way from a coin has been tried, pick the coin up and go back to the one before.
Keep going until you reach the exit.
offline.think: Your coins are a stack: the last one down is the first one up. Did you find the shortest way out, or just a way?

name: Arrays
blurb: An array is a row of slots side by side, so the computer can jump straight to any slot. The price: squeezing a new number into the middle means shuffling its neighbours along.
code: read slot i: jump straight to it
to insert at slot i:
for each slot from the end back to i
move its number one slot right
put the new number in slot i

offline.title: The egg-box shuffle
offline.need: An egg box (or 8 cups in a row), and 5 small objects
steps: Put one object in each of the first five slots of the box. Number the slots 1 to 8.
Ask a friend to name a slot. Point to it straight away. That is reading an array.
Now squeeze a new object into slot 2. You must move the objects in slots 5, 4, 3 and 2 along, one at a time, starting at the end.
Count your moves. Try inserting into slot 5 instead.
offline.think: Why must you start moving from the far end and not from slot 2? What happens if you start at the front?

name: Hash tables
blurb: A hash table does not search at all. A tiny rule, here the remainder after dividing, tells you which shelf a number lives on. To find it later, use the same rule and look on just that shelf.
code: shelf ← number mod 7
put the number on that shelf
to find: shelf ← number mod 7
check only the numbers on that shelf

offline.title: The seven-shelf shop
offline.need: Paper, a pencil and 8 numbers between 10 and 99
steps: Draw seven boxes in a row and write 0 to 6 above them. These are your shelves.
Take a number. Divide it by 7 and write the remainder in your head. Write the number in that box.
If the box already has numbers, write the new one beside them.
When all eight are filed, ask a friend to pick one. Find it by checking only one box.
offline.think: Two numbers landed on the same shelf. Is that a mistake, or just something the table has to cope with? What if all eight landed on one shelf?

name: Binary search trees
blurb: A search tree puts every number where you can find it by asking one question at a time: smaller or bigger? Each answer throws away a whole branch.
code: start at the root
compare the new number with this one
smaller: go left. bigger: go right
an empty spot? put the number there
to find: stop when the numbers match
otherwise keep going left or right

offline.title: The family tree of numbers
offline.need: Paper, a pencil and 7 numbers
steps: Write the first number at the top of the page. That is the root.
For each next number, start at the root. If it is smaller, move down-left. If it is bigger, move down-right.
When you reach an empty space, write the number there and draw a line to its parent.
Pick a number and find it by starting at the top again. Count your steps.
offline.think: What would the tree look like if you added the numbers already in order, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7? How would that change the search?

name: Dijkstra's shortest path
blurb: Keep the best distance found so far to each town. Always settle the closest town you have not settled, because nothing can beat it now. Then see if its roads give a neighbour a shorter way.
code: Home is 0; every other town is ?
pick the closest unsettled town, u
its distance is now final
for each road u – v of length len:
if dist[u] + len is shorter, update v
follow the arrows back from School

offline.title: Shortest way to school
offline.need: Paper, a pencil and a ruler
steps: Draw six dots as towns and join them with roads. Write a length on each road, 1 to 9.
Write 0 next to Home and a question mark next to every other town.
Circle the unsettled town with the smallest number. Its number is final.
For each road leaving it, add the road length to its number. If that beats the neighbour's number, cross it out and write the smaller one.
Repeat until School is circled. Trace the route back by following the roads that gave each final number.
offline.think: Why is it safe to say a town's number is final the moment it is the smallest? What would go wrong if a road could have a negative length?

name: Fewest coins
blurb: Solve the small problems first and write each answer in a table. Then build each bigger answer from answers you already wrote down. Nothing is worked out twice.
code: table[0] ← 0 coins
for each amount a from 1 up
try each coin k: table[a − k] + 1
table[a] ← the smallest of those
the answer is the last table entry

offline.title: The coin table
offline.need: Paper, a pencil and three kinds of coins, such as 1, 4 and 5 (real or drawn)
steps: Draw a row of 11 boxes, numbered 0 to 10. Write 0 in box 0.
For box 1: take away each coin that fits, look at the box that is left, and add 1. Write the smallest.
Do the same for box 2, box 3, and on up to box 10. Always look back at boxes you have already filled.
Check box 8. Is it what you get by grabbing the biggest coin first?
offline.think: The table made every answer from smaller answers. Why is that quicker than trying every possible handful of coins from scratch?

name: Counting walks
blurb: To reach a square you must come from the square above or the square on the left. So its count is those two counts added. Fill the grid from the top left and the answer appears in the last corner.
code: start square ← 1 way
blocked square ← 0 ways
for each other square in order:
ways ← ways from above + ways from left
the answer is the bottom-right square

offline.title: Count the paths
offline.need: Squared paper and a pencil
steps: Draw a grid of 4 rows and 5 columns. Shade 3 squares as blocked, but not the start or the finish.
Write 1 in the top-left square. Write 0 in every blocked square.
Fill each remaining square, row by row, with the number above it plus the number to its left.
Read the bottom-right square. That is how many different walks there are.
offline.think: What happens to the numbers just after a blocked square? How would you count walks if you could also move diagonally?

name: Sieve of Eratosthenes
blurb: A prime is a number whose only factors are 1 and itself. More than 2,000 years ago Eratosthenes found them by crossing out multiples. The numbers left uncrossed are prime.
code: write the numbers 2 … N
for p = 2, 3, … while p×p ≤ N
if p not crossed out: prime
cross out p×p, p×p+p, … ≤ N
every number left is prime

offline.title: The hundred square
offline.need: Paper, a pencil and three or four colours
steps: Draw a 10 by 10 grid and write the numbers 1 to 100, ten to a row.
Shade 1. It is not prime.
Circle 2. With one colour, shade every second number after it: 4, 6, 8 …
Circle 3, the next number that is not shaded. With a new colour, shade every third number after it.
Keep going with 5 and 7. Every number still not shaded is prime. Circle them all.
offline.think: You could stop after 7. Why do you never need to cross out with 11 when you go up to 100?

name: Euclid's GCD
blurb: The greatest common divisor is the biggest number that divides both numbers. Euclid found it by cutting the biggest squares he could off a rectangle, again and again, until nothing was left.
code: gcd(a, b)   // a × b rectangle
while b > 0
k ← how many b×b fit in a
cut off k squares
a, b ← b, a − k×b
return a

offline.title: Squares from a sheet
offline.need: Squared paper, scissors and a pencil
steps: Cut a rectangle 21 squares long and 13 squares wide out of squared paper.
Fold the short side down to make the biggest square you can. Cut it off.
Do the same with the strip that is left, and keep going.
Write down the size of every square you cut. The last, smallest square is the GCD.
Try again with 12 by 8. Can tiles of the smallest size fill the whole first rectangle?
offline.think: With 21 by 13 your squares were 13, 8, 5, 3, 2, 1, 1. Each number is the sum of the next two. Can you find a rectangle where every cut makes exactly one square?
